rationale: The hypothesis posits that a 'significant fraction' of individuals with GTPBP2 deficiency (Jaberi-Elahi syndrome) are initially misclassified as Joubert syndrome (JS) due to false-positive molar tooth sign (MTS) neuroimaging interpretation. The literature confirms that GTPBP2 pathogenic variants can indeed lead to severe cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy that mimics MTS on suboptimal axial MRI slices, leading to misdirected Joubert syndrome targeted panel testing in at least one documented case (D'Abrusco et al., 2022). However, literature reviews covering 28 reported cases (Manoochehri et al., 2024; Jaberi et al., 2016) demonstrate that the overwhelming majority of patients present with core syndromic findings—severe motor delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), intellectual disability (23/28), hypotonia (23/28), skeletal abnormalities (23/28), retinal degeneration, and neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA)—and are investigated for global neurodevelopmental disorders, ataxia, or NBIA rather than referred for ciliopathy/JS testing. Thus, while MTS false-positive misclassification is a proven diagnostic pitfall for GTPBP2, the claim that it represents a 'significant fraction' of all GTPBP2 cases is contradicted by global cohort data.

evidence.text: Whole-exome sequencing in six patients suspected of Joubert syndrome based on inappropriate recognition of the molar tooth sign (MTS) identified pathogenic variants in alternative brain malformation genes, including GTPBP2. Expert blinded pediatric neuroradiology review rejected the MTS diagnosis in five of the cases, demonstrating that cerebellar hypoplasia in GTPBP2 deficiency can be falsely interpreted as MTS.

source.title: Get your molar tooth right: Joubert syndrome misdiagnosis unmasked by whole-exome sequencing
source.quote: Here, we present six cases referred for JS genetic testing based on inappropriate recognition of MTS. While the analysis of JS-related genes was negative, whole-exome sequencing (WES) disclosed pathogenic variants in other genes causative of distinct brain malformative conditions with partial clinical and neuroradiological overlap with JS.

evidence.text: A comprehensive literature review of 28 individuals with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome reveals that the primary clinical manifestations are motor development delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), speech disorder (24/28), intellectual disability (23/28), hypotonia (23/28), skeletal problems (23/28), and visual impairment (18/28). Molar tooth sign or Joubert syndrome misclassification is not a prevalent diagnostic pathway across the broader cohort.

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome: Exploring a novel GTPBP2 mutation and a literature review
source.quote: A large numbers of patients manifest motor development delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), and speech disorder (24/28). Moreover, a significant fraction of patients suffer from intellectual disability (23/28), hypotonia (23/28), skeletal problems (23/28), and visual impairment (18/28).

evidence.text: The original description of GTPBP2-associated disease presented three affected siblings with neurodegeneration accompanied by iron deposition in the brain (NBIA-like) and retinal photoreceptor dysfunction on ERG, rather than a ciliopathy or Joubert syndrome presentation.

source.title: Identification of mutation in GTPBP2 in patients of a family with neurodegeneration accompanied by iron deposition in the brain
source.quote: The conditions in the affected individuals of the family studied may define a novel form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and GTPBP2 may be a novel neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation gene.

conflicts: D'Abrusco et al. (2022) prove that GTPBP2 cerebellar malformation can be misclassified as a molar tooth sign in centers evaluating suspected Joubert syndrome, but systematic literature review across all 28 described cases (Manoochehri et al., 2024) indicates this misinterpretation represents an isolated ascertainment occurrence rather than a 'significant fraction' of GTPBP2-deficient patients.

Clinical presentations in the larger literature focus on neurodevelopmental delay, sparse hair, early hypotonia progressing to spasticity/ataxia, and brain iron accumulation or retinal damage, diverging sharply from classic ciliopathy/Joubert syndrome cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: What proportion of negative Joubert syndrome targeted gene panel cohorts resolve to GTPBP2 variants upon reflexing to whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing?
new_directions.rationale: Directly testing JS-negative cohorts will quantify the exact diagnostic yield and misclassification rate of GTPBP2 within the ciliopathy diagnostic pipeline.

new_directions.question_text: What quantitative morphometric brain MRI criteria differentiate the pontocerebellar hypoplasia in GTPBP2 deficiency from true molar tooth sign superior cerebellar peduncle elongation?
new_directions.rationale: Standardizing imaging metrics on axial midbrain/pontine cuts will prevent false-positive MTS calls and misdirected ciliopathy gene panels.
